CanvasMAR: Improving Masked Autoregressive Video Generation With Canvas

Zian Li Affiliation: Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University Email: zian@stu.pku.edu.cn    Muhan Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding Author. Affiliation: Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University Email: muhan@pku.edu.cn
Abstract

Masked autoregressive models (MAR) have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for image and video generation, combining the flexibility of masked modeling with the potential of continuous tokenizer. However, video MAR models suffer from two major limitations: the slow-start problem, caused by the lack of a structured global prior at early sampling stages, and error accumulation across the autoregression in both spatial and temporal dimensions. In this work, we propose CanvasMAR, a novel video MAR model that mitigates these issues by introducing a canvas mechanism—a blurred, global prediction of the next frame, used as the starting point for masked generation. The canvas provides global structure early in sampling, enabling faster and more coherent frame synthesis. Furthermore, we introduce compositional classifier-free guidance that jointly enlarges spatial (canvas) and temporal conditioning, and employ noise-based canvas augmentation to enhance robustness. Experiments on the BAIR and Kinetics-600 benchmarks demonstrate that CanvasMAR produces high-quality videos with fewer autoregressive steps. Our approach achieves remarkable performance among autoregressive models on Kinetics-600 dataset and rivals diffusion-based methods.

1 Introduction

Masked generative models have achieved remarkable success in both image generation (Chang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024) and video generation (Yu et al., 2023a; Zhou et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024). By representing images as tokens and generating them set by set in a random order,11 1 For models such as MaskGiT (Chang et al., 2022), the generation order is not strictly random as noted by MAR (Li et al., 2024), since it is determined by token probabilities interpreted as confidence scores. However, we adopt a generalized notion of “random” to contrast with strictly predefined orders like raster-scan order. these models achieve higher fidelity and scalability compared to approaches that rely on predefined orders (Fan et al., 2024), such as raster-scan generation. Among these approaches, Masked Autoregressive Models (MAR) (Li et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024)22 2 Again, we adopt the generalized notion of “autoregressive” introduced in (Li et al., 2024), which treats masked generation as a form of autoregression along the spatial axis in random order. pioneer the generation of continuous image tokens with a diffusion head, in contrast to prior works that use discrete tokens (Chang et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023a), thereby eliminating the quantization errors inherent in discrete-token masked generative models and avoiding the challenges of training high-quality VQ-VAEs (Van Den Oord et al., 2017; Esser et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2023b; Han et al., 2025). This design has demonstrated strong potential both theoretically and empirically.

Extending the MAR paradigm—continuous image tokens with random-order autoregressive generation—to video generation is promising, as evidenced by several recent studies (Zhou et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). However, several key challenges remain largely unexplored. First, MAR follows the MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022) paradigm for sampling, which begins from a fully masked image and autoregressively generates tokens in a random order. At early stages, when only a few tokens have been generated, the model must only produce a small set of tokens at each step to ensure reasonable quality. The set size gradually increases as more tokens are revealed, typically following a cosine scheduling (Chang et al., 2022). This leads to a slow-start problem, which significantly hinders generation speed—particularly in video scenarios, where the additional temporal dimension exacerbates the issue. Second, extending MAR to video generation introduces two levels of autoregression: spatial random-order autoregression and temporal sequential-order autoregression. Consequently, errors accumulate across both dimensions, causing substantial quality degradation in later frames. As illustrated in Figure 1 (top row), a simple MAR model extended to video scenarios exhibits noticeable degradation within just 2 spatial autoregressive steps when generating a 16×1616\times 16 latent frame, and the problem becomes more severe as more frames are rolled out.

In this paper, we introduce CanvasMAR, a masked autoregressive video generative model that achieves robust generation quality with fewer autoregressive steps per frame. CanvasMAR generates videos via a two-level autoregressive process: in the temporal dimension, it generates frames one by one sequentially; in the space dimension, it divides each frame into image tokens and generates them set by set in random order. To address the slow-start problem for each frame, CanvasMAR first generates a blurred prediction of the next frame—referred to as the canvas-and replaces the uniform masks in conventional masked generative models with these non-uniform canvas tokens (see Figure 1, second and bottom rows). The canvas enables the model to capture the global structure of the target frame, allowing for more aggressive generation while preserving coherence. Moreover, the canvas adopts several new features that effectively mitigate error accumulation across both autoregressive dimensions and enhance the overall generation quality, including compositional classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022; Du & Kaelbling, 2024; Brooks et al., 2023) and noise augmentation (Zhang et al., 2025a). These novel designs significantly improve robustness against visual artifacts and preserve generation fidelity.

We evaluate CanvasMAR on video prediction tasks using both the lab-scale BAIR (Unterthiner et al., 2018; Ebert et al., 2017) and the large-scale real-world Kinetics-600 (Carreira et al., 2018) datasets. Remarkably, CanvasMAR demonstrates significant performance gains compared to prior autoregressive models like MAGI (Zhou et al., 2025), and rivals diffusion-based baselines. Moreover, CanvasMAR generates high-quality videos with fewer generation steps, highlighting the effectiveness of the canvas mechanism compared to its non-canvas counterpart and underscoring the importance of capturing global structure in masked generative models.

2 Related Work

Diffusion-Based Video Generative Models.

Diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable success in image generation (Ho et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020), and have since been extended to video generation by treating the temporal axis as an additional dimension alongside the spatial ones (Ho et al., 2022b; Brooks et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024). While effective, this paradigm generates entire videos in a single pass, which leads to high latency and limited interactivity—two critical drawbacks for applications such as interactive simulators and game environments (Feng et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024). To mitigate these issues, recent research has adopted an autoregressive approach, wherein videos are generated sequentially by conditioning on previously generated clean frames. This design enables interactivity and supports the generation of longer, temporally coherent videos (Ruhe et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025). Nevertheless, these methods remain diffusion-based, generating entire frames at once through iterative frame-level denoising. In contrast, token-based autoregressive models directly learn token-level distributions and produce image tokens, making them more natively compatible with language models and are thus more suitable for multi-modal model designs (Wang et al., 2024c; Jin et al., 2024).

Autoregressive Video Generation.

An alternative line of work decomposes video frames into image tokens, shifting the generative task from producing full frames to predicting sequences of tokens. Many approaches in this direction adopt quantized tokens, typically following paradigms such as next-token prediction (Yan et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024d; Wang et al., 2024c; Jin et al., 2024) or masked generative modeling (Gupta et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023a; Yu et al., 2023b; Bruce et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Villegas et al., 2022). However, as observed by Yu et al. (2023b), these paradigms rely on carefully designed and trained VQ-VAEs (Van Den Oord et al., 2017; Esser et al., 2021), which inevitably introduce quantization errors. Inspired by Masked Autoregressive Models (MAR) (Li et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024), a growing body of work—including NOVA (Deng et al., 2024), VideoMAR (Yu et al., 2025), and MAGI (Zhou et al., 2025)—adapts MAR to video generation. These methods operate by masking image tokens within frames and training the model to recover them while leveraging historical frame context.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Factorizing Video Generation

In this paper, we focus on autoregressive video generation. A video is denoted as V∈ℝN×H×W×3V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times W\times 3}, which consists of NN frames [f(1),f(2),…,f(N)][f^{(1)},f^{(2)},\ldots,f^{(N)}] of height HH and width WW. We employ latent generation (Rombach et al., 2022); however, for simplicity, we retain pixel-level notations. Autoregressive video generation models the video distribution via the following temporal factorization:

p⁡(V)=∏i=1Np⁡(f(i)∣f(1),f(2),…,f(i−1))=∏i=1Np⁡(f(i)∣f(<i)),p(V)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p\big(f^{(i)}\mid f^{(1)},f^{(2)},\ldots,f^{(i-1)}\big)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p\big(f^{(i)}\mid f^{(<i)}\big),

where f(<i)={f(1),f(2),…,f(i−1)}f^{(<i)}=\{f^{(1)},f^{(2)},\ldots,f^{(i-1)}\} denotes all preceding frames. Each frame f(i)f^{(i)} is further decomposed into a sequence of image tokens in raster order, f(i)=[x1(i),x2(i),…,xn(i)]f^{(i)}=[x^{(i)}_{1},x^{(i)}_{2},\ldots,x^{(i)}_{n}]. In standard autoregressive generation, tokens are generated in raster order token-by-token (Yan et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2022):

p⁡(f(i)∣f(<i))=∏j=1np⁡(xj(i)∣f(<i),x<j(i)),p(f^{(i)}\mid f^{(<i)})=\prod_{j=1}^{n}p\big(x^{(i)}_{j}\mid f^{(<i)},x^{(i)}_{<j}\big),

where x<j(i)={x1(i),x2(i),…,xj−1(i)}x^{(i)}_{<j}=\{x^{(i)}_{1},x^{(i)}_{2},\ldots,x^{(i)}_{j-1}\} denotes the tokens already generated within frame ii.

Following masked generative paradigms Chang et al. (2022); Li et al. (2024), we generate tokens set by set in a random order. Specifically, the nn tokens are partitioned into KK sets of sizes [n1,n2,…,nK][n_{1},n_{2},\ldots,n_{K}], with cumulative index sk=∑m=1knms_{k}=\sum_{m=1}^{k}n_{m} and s0=0s_{0}=0, sK=Ns_{K}=N. This factorization introduces spatial autoregression:

p⁡(f(i)∣f(<i))=∏k=1Kp⁡(Xk(i)∣f(<i),X1(i),X2(i),…,Xk−1(i)),p(f^{(i)}\mid f^{(<i)})=\prod_{k=1}^{K}p\big(X^{(i)}_{k}\mid f^{(<i)},X^{(i)}_{1},X^{(i)}_{2},\ldots,X^{(i)}_{k-1}\big), (1)

where each token set is defined as

Xk(i)={xτ⁡(sk−1+1)(i),xτ⁡(sk−1+2)(i),…,xτ⁡(sk)(i)},X^{(i)}_{k}=\{x^{(i)}_{\tau(s_{k-1}+1)},x^{(i)}_{\tau(s_{k-1}+2)},\ldots,x^{(i)}_{\tau(s_{k})}\},

and where τ∼𝒮N\tau\sim\mathcal{S}_{N} denotes a random permutation sampled from the symmetric group 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N}, i.e., the set of all possible permutations of the index sequence [1,2,…,N][1,2,\ldots,N]. This sampling introduces stochasticity into the generation process.

3.2 Masked Autoregressive Models with Continuous Tokens

Unlike conventional autoregressive generative models that produce quantized image tokens (Hong et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021) using categorical distributions, MAR (Li et al., 2024) directly generates continuous image tokens using a diffusion head, which models token distributions conditioned on token embeddings. Formally, the distribution in Equation 1 is further factorized as:

p⁡(Xk(i)∣f(<i),X1(i),X2(i),…,Xk−1(i)):=p⁡(Xk(i)∣Zk(i))​p​(Zk(i)∣f(<i),X1(i),X2(i),…,Xk−1(i)),p\big(X^{(i)}_{k}\mid f^{(<i)},X^{(i)}_{1},X^{(i)}_{2},\ldots,X^{(i)}_{k-1}\big):=p(X^{(i)}_{k}\mid Z^{(i)}_{k})\,p\big(Z^{(i)}_{k}\mid f^{(<i)},X^{(i)}_{1},X^{(i)}_{2},\ldots,X^{(i)}_{k-1}\big),

where Zk(i)={zτ⁡(sk−1+1)(i),zτ⁡(sk−1+2)(i),…,zτ⁡(sk)(i)}Z^{(i)}_{k}=\{z^{(i)}_{\tau(s_{k-1}+1)},z^{(i)}_{\tau(s_{k-1}+2)},\ldots,z^{(i)}_{\tau(s_{k})}\} denotes the token embeddings. The conditional distribution p⁡(Xk(i)∣Zk(i))=∏j=sk−1+1skp⁡(xj(i)∣zj(i))p(X^{(i)}_{k}\mid Z^{(i)}_{k})=\prod_{j=s_{k-1}+1}^{s_{k}}p(x^{(i)}_{j}\mid z^{(i)}_{j}) models per-token outputs given the embeddings, where the correlation between tokens are captured in the calculation of embeddings. In practice, p⁡(Zk(i)∣f(<i),X1(i),X2(i),…,Xk−1(i))p\big(Z^{(i)}_{k}\mid f^{(<i)},X^{(i)}_{1},X^{(i)}_{2},\ldots,X^{(i)}_{k-1}\big) is parameterized by a Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020), which learns token-wise embeddings, while p⁡(xj(i)∣zj(i))p(x^{(i)}_{j}\mid z^{(i)}_{j}) is modeled by a lightweight MLP-based diffusion head that conditions on zj(i)z^{(i)}_{j} to generate xj(i)x^{(i)}_{j}.

4 Methods

4.1 Factorized Temporal and Spatial Autoregression

We design our model to generate videos through a factorized temporal–spatial autoregressive framework, as illustrated in Figure 2. Specifically, CanvasMAR proceeds in two stages: 1) a temporal embedding z​t(i)∈ℝn×dzt^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, where nn denotes the number of frame tokens and dd the hidden dimension, is autoregressively generated using a Temporal ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020), taking all past frames f(<i)f^{(<i)} as context; 2) this temporal embedding is then provided as a conditioning sequence to the spatial autoregressive model, implemented as a Masked Autoregressive Model (Li et al., 2024), which generates image tokens in randomly ordered sets for the next frame f(i)f^{(i)}.

The attention mask of the Temporal ViT is designed as a hybrid structure (Deng et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025)—causal across frames and bidirectional within each frame. This design preserves temporal causality while maintaining comprehensive spatial perception within frames, which also enables KV caching, further accelerating the video generation process.

We note that this temporal-spatial factorization preserves both training and inference efficiency, in contrast to models that process temporal and spatial sequences uniformly (Zhou et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). 1) During training, tokens within each frame can be independently masked, and all masked tokens across all frames contribute to the loss in parallel, analogous to decoder-only language models. In contrast, models without factorized autoregression can only mask tokens in the last frame of a sequence when computing the loss (Yu et al., 2025), leading to inefficient training. A potential remedy, as explored in MAGI (Zhou et al., 2025), is to duplicate “clean” frames for each frame in the sequence and design a corresponding attention mask, which doubles the sequence length and substantially increases memory usage. 2) During inference, the temporally summarized embedding z​tzt captures motion information necessary to guide next-frame generation. As a result, spatial token generation only needs to attend to this fixed-length temporal embedding rather than all previously generated image tokens, whose size grows with sequence length.

4.2 Bridging Fast Temporal Autoregression and Slow Spatial Autoregression with Canvas

As shown in Figure 1, MAR suffers from a slow-start problem: the absence of an initial global estimate of the target frame significantly limits the size of the initial token set. In video generation, this issue further degrades both quality and speed. To address this, we introduce the canvas between temporal autoregression and spatial autoregression, as illustrated in Figure 2.

After obtaining the temporal embedding z​t(i)zt^{(i)}, instead of using it solely as the temporal condition for the Spatial MAR to generate the next frame, we first pass it through the Canvas ViT module. This module predicts a blurred, coarse version of the next frame z​s(i)zs^{(i)}, serving as an effective spatial condition. The Spatial MAR then receives both the temporal condition z​t(i)zt^{(i)} and the spatial canvas embedding z​s(i)zs^{(i)} to predict the next frame, as illustrated on the right side of Figure 2.

Concretely, the Canvas ViT takes the temporal representation z​t(i)zt^{(i)} together with the most recent frame f(i−1)f^{(i-1)} as input and outputs a canvas embedding z​s(i)∈ℝn×dzs^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, representing an initial guess of the next frame f(i)f^{(i)}. To supervise this process, we introduce a canvas reconstruction loss:

ℒcanvas=𝔼f(<i+1)​[∑j=1n‖fθprob​(z​sj(i))−xj(i)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\text{canvas}}=\mathbb{E}_{f^{(<i+1)}}\big[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|f^{\text{prob}}_{\theta}(zs^{(i)}_{j})-x^{(i)}_{j}\big\|_{2}^{2}\big], (2)

where z​sj(i)zs^{(i)}_{j} denotes the jj-th row of z​s(i)zs^{(i)}, and fθprobf^{\text{prob}}_{\theta} is a simple linear projection layer that supervises each patch embedding to match the corresponding patch in the ground-truth future frame.

We note that, unlike the Spatial MAR—which is inherently slower and stochastic—the Canvas ViT is fast and deterministic: given the same temporal embedding z​t(i)zt^{(i)} and previous frame f(i−1)f^{(i-1)}, it always produces the same canvas.

Theoretically, the optimal solution of Canvas ViT learns to approximate the expected future frame 𝔼f(i)∼p⁡(f(i)∣f(<i))​[f(i)]\mathbb{E}_{f^{(i)}\sim p(f^{(i)}\mid f^{(<i)})}[f^{(i)}] given previous frames f(<i)f^{(<i)}, effectively producing a superposition of plausible outcomes. This provides the Spatial MAR with an efficient and informative initialization, enabling it to maintain global coherence early on and quickly “collapse” onto one of the plausible future frames through Spatial MAR.

4.3 Mitigating Error Accumulation in Two-Level Autoregression

Direct autoregression typically suffers from error accumulation (Song et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). In our setting, there are two levels of autoregression—temporal over frames and spatial over image tokens—which compounds the issue. We introduce two techniques to alleviate this problem.

4.3.1 Canvas Augmentation

The canvas is predicted in one pass, unlike iterative generative models that refine outputs across multiple iterations. This introduces two potential sources of error: 1) inaccuracies in the previously generated frame may mislead the Canvas ViT, compounding errors in the next canvas prediction; and 2) even with an accurate previous frame, the one-pass Canvas ViT may produce overly blurred or imprecise canvases, confusing the Spatial MAR and amplifying artifacts.

To mitigate these effects, we adopt a noise-based augmentation strategy inspired by cascaded generation methods (Zhang et al., 2025a; Ho et al., 2022a). Specifically, when feeding the most recent frame f(i−1)f^{(i-1)} into the Canvas ViT, we augment it with Gaussian noise:

faug(i−1)=f(i−1)⋅(1−r)+ϵ⋅r,f^{(i-1)}_{\text{aug}}=f^{(i-1)}\cdot(1-r)+\epsilon\cdot r, (3)

where ϵ\epsilon is random Gaussian noise and rr is an interpolation coefficient. Similarly, we perturb the canvas embedding:

z​saug(i)=z​s(i)⋅(1−r′)+ϵ′⋅r′,zs^{(i)}_{\text{aug}}=zs^{(i)}\cdot(1-r^{\prime})+\epsilon^{\prime}\cdot r^{\prime}, (4)

where ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime} and r′r^{\prime} denote another Gaussian noise and interpolation coefficient. These augmentations simulate instability in previously generated frames and canvases, forcing both the Canvas ViT and the Spatial MAR to maintain robustness to imperfect conditions. During training, we sample r,r′∼𝒰⁡(0,0.8)r,r^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,0.8), while during inference we fix rr and r′r^{\prime} to a number between [0.3,0.6][0.3,0.6].

4.3.2 Compositional Classifier-Free Guidance for Temporal and Spatial Conditions

For the Spatial MAR, the generative distribution is defined as p⁡(f(i)∣z​s(i),z​t(i))p(f^{(i)}\mid zs^{(i)},zt^{(i)}), where z​s(i)zs^{(i)} denotes the spatial condition (the canvas) and z​t(i)zt^{(i)} denotes the temporal condition. These two conditions naturally induce two forms of classifier-free guidance (CFG).

We decompose the distribution as:

p⁡(f(i)∣z​s(i),z​t(i))∝p⁡(f(i))​p​(z​t(i)∣f(i))​p​(z​s(i)∣f(i),z​t(i)),p(f^{(i)}\mid zs^{(i)},zt^{(i)})\propto p(f^{(i)})\,p(zt^{(i)}\mid f^{(i)})\,p(zs^{(i)}\mid f^{(i)},zt^{(i)}),

and apply compositional CFG (Du & Kaelbling, 2024; Brooks et al., 2023) to up-weight both the spatial and temporal posteriors:

p(ws,wt)​(f(i)∣z​s(i),z​t(i))=p⁡(f(i))​p​(z​t(i)∣f(i))wt​p​(z​s(i)∣f(i),z​t(i))ws,p^{(w_{s},w_{t})}(f^{(i)}\mid zs^{(i)},zt^{(i)})=p(f^{(i)})\,p(zt^{(i)}\mid f^{(i)})^{w_{t}}\,p(zs^{(i)}\mid f^{(i)},zt^{(i)})^{w_{s}}, (5)

where wsw_{s} and wtw_{t} denote the guidance scales for the spatial and temporal conditions, respectively. Intuitively, wsw_{s} and wtw_{t} enhance the likelihood of the generated frame f(i)f^{(i)} conforming to the spatial prior zs(i)z_{s}^{(i)} and the temporal consistency constraint zt(i)z_{t}^{(i)}, respectively.

By Bayes’ theorem, the corresponding score of the guided log-probability can be expressed as

∇f(i)​log​p(ws,wt)​(f(i)∣zs(i),zt(i))\displaystyle\nabla_{f^{(i)}}\log p^{(w_{s},w_{t})}\big(f^{(i)}\mid z_{s}^{(i)},z_{t}^{(i)}\big) =∇f(i)​log​p​(f(i))\displaystyle=\nabla_{f^{(i)}}\log p\big(f^{(i)}\big) (6)
+wt​(∇f(i)​log​p​(f(i)∣zt(i))−∇f(i)​log​p​(f(i)))\displaystyle+w_{t}\Big(\nabla_{f^{(i)}}\log p\big(f^{(i)}\mid z_{t}^{(i)}\big)-\nabla_{f^{(i)}}\log p\big(f^{(i)}\big)\Big)
+ws​(∇f(i)​log​p​(f(i)∣zs(i),zt(i))−∇f(i)​log​p​(f(i)∣zt(i))),\displaystyle+w_{s}\Big(\nabla_{f^{(i)}}\log p\big(f^{(i)}\mid z_{s}^{(i)},z_{t}^{(i)}\big)-\nabla_{f^{(i)}}\log p\big(f^{(i)}\mid z_{t}^{(i)}\big)\Big),

where three (un)conditional score terms jointly contribute to the final gradient. To learn the classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022; Brooks et al., 2023), during training: (1) with 5% probability, we replace the spatial condition with a uniform mask (Chang et al., 2022); (2) with 5% probability, we replace the temporal sequence condition with a learnable vector augmented by sinusoidal positional encoding. and (3) with 5% probability, we remove both simultaneously. This encourages the model to generalize effectively under varying conditional contexts.

5 Experiments

Model Implementation

We implement the model based on the NOVA (Deng et al., 2024) codebase with several modifications, in addition to those stated in previous sections: 1) using a flow-head trained with flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022) instead of DDPM (Ho et al., 2020); 2) for the Spatial DiT, adopting a design similar to MM-DiT (Esser et al., 2024), which employs separate MLPs for canvas/mask and clean tokens; and 3) omitting the Scaling and Shift Layer for the temporal embedding (Deng et al., 2024).

Tasks and Datasets

We primarily evaluate the proposed architecture on video prediction tasks, where one or multiple initial frames are provided and the task is to predict subsequent frames. We use two datasets of different scales and complexity: 1) BAIR. The BAIR dataset (Unterthiner et al., 2018; Ebert et al., 2017) is a toy benchmark designed for single-frame conditional video generation. It contains 43K training videos and 256 evaluation videos, depicting a robot arm pushing objects within a static camera view. We train our models at a resolution of 64×6464\times 64. 2) Kinetics-600. The Kinetics-600 dataset (Carreira et al., 2018) is a large-scale collection of diverse real-world videos spanning 600 human action categories. It contains approximately 400K training clips and serves as a challenging benchmark for large-scale video generation. For this dataset, we train at 128×128128\times 128 resolution. We evaluate all models using the Frechet Video Distance (FVD) (Carreira et al., 2018) metric on 64×6464\times 64 resolution videos, following the conventional evaluation protocol (Zhou et al., 2025). Generated videos larger than this resolution are bilinearly downsampled for evaluation.

5.1 Ablation Study

Effectiveness of the Canvas.

Since the canvas mechanism is the core design of CanvasMAR, we first investigate its impact. To this end, we train a model identical to CanvasMAR but without the canvas component, which effectively resembles to NOVA (Deng et al., 2024). We then compare both models under identical conditions. Quantitative results (see Figure 3(a)) show that the canvas-equipped model consistently outperforms its non-canvas counterpart across all autoregressive step counts, with the largest improvement under small step counts (e.g., 3–6). Qualitative comparisons in Figure 4 demonstrate that the model without the canvas struggles to maintain global structure and object coherence, while the canvas-based model preserves spatial and temporal consistency.

Compositional Classifier-Free Guidance.

We further evaluate the compositional classifier-free guidance (CFG) introduced in Section 3. Based on Equation 5, wtw_{t} improves temporal consistency, whereas wsw_{s} strengthens the spatial prior. Qualitative illustrations of the effects of both coefficients are shown in the left side of Figure 5.

As shown in Figure 3(b), increasing the temporal guidance scale to wt=1.1w_{t}=1.1 yields the best performance when the spatial guidance scale is fixed at ws=1.0w_{s}=1.0. Holding wt=1.1w_{t}=1.1 and further increasing wsw_{s} continues to improve results, confirming that both temporal and spatial CFG components effectively contribute to generation quality. Based on these results, we set the spatial CFG wsw_{s} to a relatively larger value (2.0∼3.02.0\sim 3.0) and the temporal CFG wtw_{t} to a smaller value (1.1∼1.21.1\sim 1.2).

5.2 System-Level Comparisons

We compare CanvasMAR with well-known models, including both diffusion-based and autoregressive video generation methods. We categorize each model as diffusion or autoregressive by its frame-level generation mechanism-generating frames as a whole, or decomposing it into image tokens. Such frame-level generation mechanism more directly determines visual quality characteristics than its temporal generation paradigm (i.e., generating an entire video at once versus rolling out frames sequentially).

As shown in Table 1, CanvasMAR achieves the second-best performance on BAIR among all autoregressive models. We note that MAGVIT is autoregressive only in the spatial domain (i.e., generating image tokens), but not in the temporal domain—it generates all frames simultaneously, without enforcing temporal causality. This naturally provides advantages in capturing temporal dependencies, especially in such simplified scenarios, yet with higher latency since users cannot see videos until all frames are generated.

On the larger and more challenging Kinetics-600 dataset, Figure 5 (right) presents several qualitative examples. The canvas is first predicted, producing a blurred representation that captures the global structure of the upcoming frame. Subsequently, the MAR module refines this prediction by adding high-frequency details. Quantitatively, our method achieves strong performance among autoregressive approaches, trailing only MAGVIT-v2 (Yu et al., 2023b), which generates all frames simultaneously as previously discussed, and employs a more advanced autoencoder. In contrast, our model generates frames sequentially and relies on a simple non-causal autoencoder from Song et al. (2025), which introduces additional challenges for the latent generative model. We also note that MAGI (Zhou et al., 2025) serves as a closely related baseline—MAR-like but without using the Canvas mechanism—underscoring the effectiveness of our proposed design. Moreover, our approach rivals state-of-the-art diffusion models on this demanding dataset, demonstrating the potential of such autoregressive paradigm.

Note that a direct comparison of autoregressive steps across models is not particularly meaningful, since different methods employ distinct tokenizers that result in varying latent representations. For instance, MAGI (Zhou et al., 2025) tokenizes 17×256×25617\times 256\times 256 Kinetics-600 videos using the OmniTokenizer (Wang et al., 2024a) into a latent space of 5×32×325\times 32\times 32, and generates each frame with 64 autoregressive steps. In contrast, we tokenize 17×128×12817\times 128\times 128 videos into 5×16×165\times 16\times 16 and generate each frame with 12 autoregressive steps. Although we use fewer steps, the corresponding latent space is also smaller. Therefore, rather than directly comparing step counts with other methods, this section demonstrates how Canvas enables MAR-like methods to achieve superior performance, and how it largely maintains performance when the iteration steps are further reduced, as shown in the last two rows in Table 1.

5.3 Next-Group Frame Prediction

In diffusion-based autoregressive models (Yin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025), predicting multiple upcoming frames jointly is common. However, for token-based autoregressive models, next-group prediction often leads to performance degradation. For example, NOVA (Deng et al., 2024) generates frames one at a time.

With the introduction of the canvas, we find next-group frame prediction to be stable, enabling faster generation with small quality loss. To achieve this, we slightly modify the architectures by appending KK canvas heads, each implemented as a two-layer MLP, to the output of the Canvas ViT. We also add lightweight temporal attention layers among spatial layers every 4 layers, following the decomposed attention design of Gupta et al. (2024), to ensure temporal consistency. These canvas heads provide the spatial conditioning canvases for generating the next KK frames within the Spatial MAR.

Empirically, we finetune a next-group frame prediction model (with a group size of 2) from a well-trained next-frame prediction model on BAIR dataset, requiring only about 10%10\% of the original training cost to converge, indicating that substantial prior knowledge can be transferred between next-frame and next-group settings.

As shown in Figure 6(b), the next-2-frame model exhibits substantial speedup at smaller batch sizes compared to the next-frame model and converges to similar throughput at higher batch sizes. This occurs because, when the batch size becomes large, both the next-frame and next-2-frame models fully utilize the available GPU resources. Because of KV caching, they reach a similar level of parallel efficiency. In practical scenarios, however, users typically need to generate only few videos and expect low latency, where the next-2-frame prediction model proves particularly advantageous. Furthermore, we train a next-2-frame prediction model without using the canvas, whose performance is illustrated by the purple curve. Our canvas-based model achieves significantly better performance when transferred to next-group prediction, as the canvas provides strong structural priors that guide future-frame prediction under such aggressive sampling settings.

6 Limitations

Despite its remarkable performance demonstrated in previous sections, we identify several limitations of CanvasMAR. First, when predicting videos with significant motion, CanvasMAR tends to produce severely distorted results, as shown in Figure 7. One reason for this is that the initially predicted canvas is overly blurred for high-dynamic videos, which misleads the Spatial MAR, as it still lacks the capability to correct such artifacts. Scaling up the model may improve its self-correction ability given the techniques introduced in Section 4.3, especially considering that the largest Spatial MAR model we currently use has only half the layers of NOVA (Deng et al., 2024).

Second, while enlarging temporal classifier-free guidance sometimes improves perceptual quality and aesthetic scores (Huang et al., 2024) in case studies, it typically negatively affects the FVD score of generated videos. This discrepancy partly arises from the unreliability of FVD (Skorokhodov et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2024), which is often biased and misaligned with human perception. More comprehensive evaluations using modern metrics like VBench (Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025) are needed, though current baselines on these metrics are very limited, and most competing methods remain closed-source (Yu et al., 2023a). Future research should extend CanvasMAR to text-to-video generation, where modern evaluation protocols are more prevalent.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we presented CanvasMAR, a masked autoregressive video generation framework that enhances both quality and efficiency through the introduction of a canvas-based conditioning mechanism. By generating a blurred global estimate of the next frame before spatial token generation, CanvasMAR bridges the gap between fast temporal and slow spatial autoregression, mitigating the slow-start problem that affects conventional MAR models. Combined with compositional classifier-free guidance and noise-based canvas augmentation, our approach effectively reduces error accumulation across frames and preserves global coherence throughout long sequences. Experiments on BAIR and Kinetics-600 confirm that CanvasMAR achieves competitive or superior FVD scores with fewer autoregressive steps, outperforming most of prior autoregressive baselines. Future work will explore scaling CanvasMAR to text-conditioned and multi-modal settings.

Appendix A Experiment Details

Sampling Methods

As noted by Skorokhodov et al. (2022), the sampling procedure can significantly influence FVD scores. To ensure a fair comparison, we adhere closely to the sampling strategies used in prior work:

  • •

    BAIR: For each of the 256 test videos, we use the first frame as the conditioning input and the subsequent 16-frame segment as the real distribution. For each conditioning frame, we generate 100 synthetic 16-frame video clips, resulting in a total of 256×100256\times 100 generated clips in the fake distribution.

    Following Yu et al. (2023a), we also report the debiased FVD, which is computed by randomly sampling one frame from each test video as the conditioning input and defining the real distribution accordingly. This process is repeated 100 times per test video, resulting in also a total of 256×100256\times 100 generated clips in the fake distribution. Since this approach mitigates bias, we report the debiased FVD in all cases except for system-level comparisons for fairness.

  • •

    Kinetics-600: We randomly sample 50K test videos from the test dataset and, for each, select a random 16-frame clips for defining the real-distribution and taking the 5-frame conditions for generating one 16-frame video clips in the fake distribution.

Training and Model Details.

All models are trained on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Comprehensive model configurations and hyperparameters are listed in Table 2.
